newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CENBANK LEAVES INTEREST RATES UNCHANGED.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CENBANK LEAVES INTEREST RATES UNCHANGED.

text.p: The Czech National Bank said on Thursday that the central bank's governing board did not consider a change in its key interest rates despite new M2 data showing a marked slowing in money supply growth.
"A change in interest rates has not been discussed at today's board meeting," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters following the meeting.

Earlier, the central bank reported that M2 growth slowed to 9.2 percent at the end of December from 11.3 percent in November, year-on-year, excluding large deposits connected to the 1995 equity expansion of SPT Telecom a.s..
With the SPT factored in from 1995, M2 growth slowed to 7.8 percent from 9.7 in November.

Market speculation about a possible rate cut had been high after Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus on Tuesday criticised the central bank for possibly going to far in tightening monetary policy last summer.
Last June the CNB raised its key discount rate a full percentage point to 10.5 percent and raised minimum reserve requirements.
But Svehla said the data indicated that M2 data released on Thursday did not necessarily suggest that the central bank had more room to ease monetary policy.
"This is the past -- the end of last year. To adjust monetary policy it is necessary to watch some future developments. This (M2) is no reason for anything," Svehla said.

When asked if the central bank saw any indication of a change in the M2 trend, Svehla said: "We are still somewhere around nine percent growth... and we lowered our target in money supply growth to eight to 12 percent."
"That means that we are still within the range that we projected."
Industrial output in January contracted 3.9 percent, year-on-year, according to data released earlier this week.
Klaus said that a slowing in growth may have been a high price to pay for the slowing in inflation which the central bank tightening measures produced.
"The decline of growth is multi-dimensional, not only monetary policy is the reason, but other, and perhaps more important factors are engaged," Svehla said.
Czech February inflation slowed to 7.3 percent year-on-year from 9.1 percent for the same month in 1996, but GDP growth has slowed to below four percent.
The central bank has pointed at slowing in demand for Czech exports, especially in the European Union and neighbouring Germany, as one of several reasons for the slower growth.
Svehla said that no other decisions were taken at the central bank's meeting.
